item.title: US stocks sink as AI and chips tumble
item.description:
US stocks closed lower Wednesday, with AI and semiconductor shares taking a particularly hard hit. The Nasdaq Composite recorded its worst day since July 23, while the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 posted their largest declines since July 29.

The hotter-than-expected CPI report provided an uncomfortable backdrop. Headline inflation rose 3.7% year over year versus 3.6% expected, keeping inflation and the Fed’s next move firmly in focus. Treasury yields moved sharply higher following the release, adding pressure on growth-stock valuations, but did move back lower off their highs as stocks retreated and they found a safe haven bid.  The 2 year is still 1.9 basis points higher at 4.812%, but the 10 year is trading down -1.9 basis points at 5.198%. The US 2 year yield reached a high of 4.95% while the US 10 year yield reached a high of 5.329%.

The Dow held up relatively well, falling just 0.09%. However, the selling extended beyond technology, with the Russell 2000 losing nearly 2%. Traders now turn to Thursday’s September PPI report at 8:30 AM ET for the next inflation test. The combination of the CPI and the PPI will give traders and Fed officials a good read on the overall core PCE data.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: Down 48.98 points, or 0.09%, at 51,626.17.

  • S&P 500: Down 86.51 points, or 1.11%, at 7,718.94.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 511.51 points, or 1.88%, at 26,692.87.

  • Russell 2000: Down 53.84 points, or 1.93%, at 2,729.53.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 618.66 points, or 2.02%, at 29,950.82.

AI and chip stocks take the brunt

There were few places to hide within the AI, semiconductor and related infrastructure names. A number of shares fell more than 5%, with some suffering double-digit percentage declines.

Among the hardest hit:

  • CoreWeave: −15.46%.

  • Nebius: −10.08%.

  • Credo Technology: −9.62%.

  • Lumentum: −9.28%.

  • Coherent: −9.19%.

  • Bloom Energy: −9.15%.

  • Marvell Technology: −8.72%.

  • Astera Labs: −7.72%.

  • Arm Holdings: −6.81%.

  • GE Vernova: −6.20%.

  • SK Hynix: −6.06%.

  • Monolithic Power Systems: −5.79%.

  • AMD: −5.73%.

  • SanDisk: −5.33%.

Even some of the better performers in the group suffered meaningful losses. Texas Instruments fell 2.50%, KLA declined 2.82%, and Broadcom lost 3.10%.

That tells you something about the selling pressure. When a decline of 2.5%–3% puts a stock among the better performers, sellers have a firm grip on the group.

Apple stands alone among the Magnificent Seven

Apple managed to buck the selling, but the other six names finished lower:

  • Apple: +0.50%.

  • Alphabet: −1.74%.

  • Amazon: −1.74%.

  • Microsoft: −1.80%.

  • Tesla: −2.15%.

  • Nvidia: −3.16%.

  • Meta: −3.27%.

Nasdaq 100: Sellers take more control below the 200-hour moving average

The Nasdaq 100 closed at 29,950.82, below its 200-hour moving average near 30,145. That break shifts the shorter-term technical bias further toward the sellers.

The burden is now on the buyers to get the price back above that moving average—and stay above it. Until they can do that, rebounds remain vulnerable to sellers leaning against the level.

On the downside, the next major target is the 100-day moving average near 29,618.83. The rising lower channel trendline is also nearby, making that area an important battleground.

If buyers defend that area, they can try to stabilize the decline. A sustained break below both the moving average and trendline would increase the bearish bias, with the 28,822.67–28,953.26 swing area becoming a broader downside target.

Conversely, reclaiming 30,145 would ease some immediate pressure. Buyers would then need to work back through the resistance area around 30,634.67–30,762.20, which includes the 100-hour moving average near 30,665.

Sellers have made their move. Buyers need to show they can take something back.

The trading lesson: Let the levels define the risk

A sharp decline does not automatically make a stock or index a bargain. For a beginner trader, the more useful question is: What would tell me the selling pressure is easing?

For the Nasdaq 100, recovering and holding above the broken 200-hour moving average would be an initial improvement. Finding buyers near the 100-day moving average would be another development to watch.

Support gives traders a place to measure risk. The price still has to hold it.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia jobs preview: NAB sees 20,000 gain, unemployment steady at 4.6%
item.description:
With NAB, Westpac and consensus all at 20,000 and three major banks seeing unemployment at 4.6%, the bar for a surprise sits mainly in the jobless rate. A drop to 4.5% would revive the case for further RBA tightening and could support the Australian dollar and short-dated yields. A rise to 4.7% would push the other way, adding weight to the view that four hikes are already doing enough. NAB’s view that the cooling is supply-led also matters for rates: rising labour force participation eases wage pressure without signalling a hiring slump, which gives the RBA less reason to sound alarmed about growth.

-

NAB thinks August’s jobless jump was partly a statistical quirk, but not enough of one to drag the rate back to 4.5% this month.

Summary:

  • Australia’s September labour force data are due at 11.30am Sydney time Thursday (0030 GMT Thursday, 8.30pm US Eastern Wednesday)
  • NAB forecasts employment up 20,000, matching Westpac and consensus, with CBA lower at about 10,000
  • NAB sees unemployment holding at 4.6%, with some risk of a lower reading
  • That would sit marginally above the RBA’s 4.5% fourth-quarter forecast, which NAB says would not materially change the central bank’s assessment unless unemployment keeps surprising higher
  • NAB said August’s jump looked partly due to residual seasonality and ABS methodology changes, raising the prospect of some payback
  • A low-unemployment survey group rotating out, and rounding, keep NAB from making 4.5% its base case

National Australia Bank expects Australia’s September labour force figures to show employment rising by 20,000 and the unemployment rate holding at 4.6%, with some risk of a lower reading. The data are due at 11.30am Sydney time on Thursday, which is 0030 GMT and 8.30pm US Eastern time on Wednesday.

NAB’s forecast matches Westpac’s and the market consensus. CBA expects a softer gain of about 10,000. All three banks see unemployment unchanged.

A 4.6% reading would leave the jobless rate slightly above the 4.5% fourth-quarter projection in the Reserve Bank of Australia’s August Statement on Monetary Policy, its quarterly economic outlook. NAB does not expect that gap to materially shift the RBA’s view of the labour market unless unemployment keeps surprising higher through to year-end. The bank said much of the recent cooling reflects more people entering the workforce rather than weaker hiring, and that indicators of labour demand remain resilient.

NAB said August’s jump in unemployment appeared partly due to residual seasonality and partly due to methodology changes. Residual seasonality refers to seasonal patterns that the adjustment process did not fully strip out. The methodology changes were made under the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ Labour Force Modernisation project. Together, these raise the prospect of some payback this month.

Two factors stop NAB from making a 4.5% print its base case. First, the eighth of the survey sample rotating out this month has an unusually low unemployment rate, so its departure tends to push the measured rate higher. Second, August’s rate was about 4.65% before rounding. It could therefore fall almost a full tenth of a percentage point and still be reported as 4.6%.

The result feeds directly into the debate over whether the RBA, having lifted its cash rate four times to 4.60%, needs to go further. On NAB’s reading, a steady 4.6% would not be enough to shift that assessment. A run of upside surprises in unemployment through to year-end would be. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas market news wrap: Hot CPI upends markets
item.description:
• US September CPI 3.7% vs 3.6% expected
  • Canada August building permits rise 8.8% vs 2.0% expected
  • Fed's Beige Book: Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
  • Fed’s Goolsbee: CPI was discouraging, more bad months would be unacceptable

Markets:

  • WTI crude oil up 98-cents to $95.12
  • US 10-year yields down 2.3 bps to 5.19%
  • Gold down $54 to $4103
  • USD leads, GBP lags
  • S&P 500 down 1.2%

The US CPI report threw gasoline on the debate about an October rate just as the Fed nears the blackout period. Market pricing now sits at 37% after briefly rising above 50% in the aftermath of the CPI report that was hot across the board. There were no big caveats in the data that was generally 0.1 pp above expectations. Comments from Goolsbee late in the day did seem to push back on the idea of a hike this month, saying "more bad months would be unacceptable" but it's been 5 years of CPI above target and you have to wonder how many bad months that is already. In any case, the Fed chair speaks late on Thursday and that's going to be a big one.

In terms of market reaction, it was no surprise to see USD rally, stocks fall (it took awhile) and precious metals drop (silver down 6%). What was surprising was the bond market as Treasury yields initially shot much higher only to fade, then reverse later. US 2-year yields rose as high as 4.95% only to finish at 4.81%, suggesting that the market doesn't see a big FOMC repricing. Further out the curve, yields finished the day lower, suggesting the possibility of over-tightening.

Of course, the CPI report didn't happen in a vacuum and the AI trade remains dominant throughout markets. Tech stocks got hit hard on fresh worries about overspending and profitability. Notably, it's the bond market that's pushing some of the worries as Oracle borrowing costs and CDS rise. Another report highlights that CoreWeave yields are nearing 15%, taking down the stocks of the neoclouds. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Goolsbee: CPI was discouraging, more bad months would be unacceptable
item.description:
• CPI data was ‘discouraging’
  • Service inflation in CPI was a concern
  • Key to focus on trend of inflation, not one report
  • Hearing about cost and prices from contacts, not hearing about worries about recession
  • Hopes energy will fade soon from inflation data
  • The economy has work to do on the inflation side
  • Is not a fan of telegraphing Fed moves ahead of meetings
  • There is no ambiguity for Fed if economy is solid and inflation is high
  • Fed must prevent the build up of overheating
  • Is more optimistic about outlook relative to other Fed officials
  • Evidence building inflation hasn’t been transitory amid continued shocks
  • Need to keep a close eye on service sector inflation
  • More bad months of inflation would be unacceptable
  • Fed will get inflation back to 2%
  • Doesn’t want to tie hands on monetary policy outlook
  • If current inflation levels hold policy would need to address that
  • Consumers, GDP and investment levels have been strong
  • AI hype could cause even more tech sector investment, would risk overheating
  • Slowdown in AI investment doesn’t have to mean recession
  • Want to keep eye on financial stability implications of AI investment

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called today’s CPI data discouraging and said that if current inflation levels hold, policy would need to address that.

He said evidence is building that inflation hasn’t been transitory amid continued shocks and that more bad months of inflation would be unacceptable. He flagged services inflation as a concern and said he hopes energy will fade from the data soon, though he stressed the importance of focusing on the trend rather than any one report.

Goolsbee said there’s no ambiguity for the Fed when the economy is solid and inflation is high, and that the Fed must prevent overheating from building. Consumers, GDP and investment have been strong, and his contacts are talking about costs and prices, not recession. He said he’s more optimistic about the outlook than other Fed officials.

On AI, he warned that hype could drive even more tech investment and risk overheating, and said the Fed needs to watch the financial stability implications. A slowdown in AI investment wouldn’t necessarily mean a recession, he added.

Goolsbee said he doesn’t want to tie his hands on policy and isn’t a fan of telegraphing moves ahead of meetings. After today's CPI report,the market is pricing in a 40% chance of a hike later this month. We will hear from Warsh late tomorrow then the Fed goes into blackout on Saturday.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold sellers press toward last week’s low. Can buyers hold support?
item.description:
Gold buyers had their shot. Monday’s rebound stalled ahead of the familiar swing level near $4,226.81, and today the price has moved back below both its 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages. The focus has shifted from breaking resistance to defending support.

The fall has taken gold to $4073.49. The current price is at $4092, down around $68.83, or 1.65%. Last week’s low at $4,066.21 is now within reach. That is the next test for sellers, and a level where buyers can try to stall the decline with risk defined against it.

Buyers could not get through the swing ceiling

The $4,226.81 area has been a recurring decision level on the supplied chart, with reactions going back to June (see red numbered circles). More recently, it has acted as resistance on October 2 and again this week on Tuesday (Oct 12).

Monday’s rally fell short of that ceiling. Buyers could not get above and stay above. That failure kept the recovery within the broader decline from the late-August high.

Today’s break below the hourly moving averages added to the bearish development. At the chart snapshot, those levels are:

  • 200-hour moving average: $4,153.42
  • 100-hour moving average: $4,163.43

The price is below both. That keeps the short-term bias in the sellers’ favor. Buyers need to get back above that area and stay above to show they are taking more control.

Last week’s low is the next downside test

The immediate downside target is $4,066.21. A target is also a decision area. Sellers may take some profit there, while buyers may look to stop the decline.

Holding that low would give buyers a foothold. They would still need to reclaim the hourly moving averages to improve the technical picture.

If sellers push below $4,066.21 and stay below, the next support areas come into focus:

  • $4,000 to $4,018.79: The upper highlighted swing-support zone, including the natural $4,000 level.
  • $3,942.71 to $3,959.37: The lower highlighted swing-support zone.

Those are conditional targets if support gives way. The reaction at each area will provide the next clue.

What would improve the outlook for buyers?

The first step is to stop the decline. The next is to reclaim $4,153.42 to $4,163.43, the area defined by the two hourly moving averages.

A sustained move above both would weaken the immediate bearish bias and put the $4,226.81 swing ceiling back in play. Beyond that, the 100-day moving average near $4,256.20 is another recovery hurdle.

Until those steps occur, a bounce remains a recovery within a bearish setup.

Trading education: Yesterday’s support can fail today

The hourly moving averages helped buyers defend the price yesterday. Today, the price is below them. That change matters.

A technical level gives traders a place to judge the price action and define risk. It does not guarantee that support will hold on the next test. When price moves below support, traders need to recognize the change and adjust their bias.

The same lesson applies to $4,066.21. A bounce would show that buyers are defending the low. A sustained break below would give sellers more control.

For now, sellers retain the bias below the hourly moving averages. Buyers need to hold support, then get back above and stay above those moving averages to improve the outlook.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Beige Book: Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
item.description:
• Two districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight and three no change. In August, 10 grew and two were unchanged.
  • Most districts reported little or no change in consumer spending.
  • Employment was little changed: three districts saw modest gains, five slight and four no change.
  • Three districts reported robust price growth, eight moderate and one modest.
  • Four districts said the pace of price increases picked up.
  • The outlook remains positive, but expectations are for slight growth, weighted toward manufacturing.

The October Beige Book shows an economy losing a step while inflation pressures intensify. The national summary dropped its headline characterization of activity entirely. August said activity “increased modestly”; this report simply tallies the districts and notes that reports outside of manufacturing “indicate little growth overall.” Philadelphia and New York both slowed to slight growth from modest, while Chicago slipped to flat. Manufacturing is doing the heavy lifting, led by a sharp pickup in Dallas along with continued strength in data centers, power generation and defense.

The consumer has stalled. August described spending as growing slightly; now most districts report little or no change, and more than half said spending was being driven by high-income households. The strain is spreading up the income ladder. San Francisco said pressure on lower-income families has spread to middle-income households, and New York noted rising 401(k) hardship withdrawals and earned-wage advances. In Cleveland, a record 87% of surveyed nonprofits said their clients’ finances deteriorated. Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco all flagged a drop in Canadian tourists.

Prices are the biggest shift. In August, only one district reported robust price growth and only one said the pace had accelerated. Now it’s three and four, respectively. Higher oil prices showed up in every district report, with diesel the most commonly cited cost. The forward-looking language is more concerning for the Fed: firms expect further increases as hedges and fixed contracts expire and get repriced. Philadelphia’s future prices indexes are among the highest readings in 35 years, and a New York food manufacturer said it hadn’t seen such broad-based pressures since the pandemic. Consumer-facing firms still can’t pass costs through, so margins are getting squeezed.

Hiring was marginally better than August, but real wages are a growing issue. Boston staffing contacts said raises are lagging inflation, and cost-of-living demands came up in several districts. AI also featured more prominently, with five districts reporting firms trimming staff through attrition, delaying hiring or planning fewer new jobs.

Higher rates are a new theme. Rising mortgage rates slowed housing further in Philadelphia, Kansas City said CRE loan spreads rose substantially, and Dallas bankers turned pessimistic, citing the Mideast conflict, inflation and the increase in the fed funds rate.

The FOMC meets Oct. 27-28 and along with today's CPI report, this adds to the case for hiking rates. We will hear from Chair Warsh late tomorrow.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers defend moving average resistance. What does that teach traders?
item.description:
US stocks are lower, Treasury yields are higher, and oil prices are higher. That risk-off backdrop is weighing on Bitcoin. But for traders, the technical levels help answer the more practical questions: Who has control? Where is the risk? What needs to happen next?

The moving average gives traders a decision point

On the four-hour chart, Bitcoin fell below its 100-bar moving average on October 7. After finding support near $80,106 on October 8, the price rebounded but stalled against that moving average on October 12 and again today.

Why does that matter?

A moving average can act as support when the price is above it and resistance when the price is below it. In this case, the rebounds more recently in Bitcoin gave buyers opportunities to reclaim the 200 and the 100 bar moving averages on the 4-hour chart. The 200 bar MA (green line), was broken but sellers leaned near the 100 bar MA (blue line).  Buyers could not get and stay above the higher MA. Sellers leaned against the level and pushed the price back lower.

The buyers had their shot. They missed.

For sellers, that moving average provides a reference point to define risk. Stay below keeps the bearish bias intact. Move above and stay above, and the reason for leaning against that resistance begins to weaken.

The moving average does not guarantee the next move. It gives traders a level against which to judge the price action.

Support is an area—not just one price

Today’s low has reached $81,570, bringing Bitcoin closer to the swing support area between $80,106 and $81,183.

A swing area is a zone where the price has previously attracted buying or selling interest (see the lower yellow area on the chart above). Traders watch it because those past reactions identify a place where another battle may develop.

There are two steps to watch:

  • Below $81,183: The price enters the support area. Sellers gain ground, but the broader range remains intact.

  • Below $80,106: The price breaks the floor of the range that has confined Bitcoin since September 19. Staying below would strengthen the bearish case and open the door for further selling.

That distinction matters. Moving into support is different from breaking through support.

A break needs follow-through

If Bitcoin breaks below $80,106, traders will watch whether the price can stay below that level and extend lower. A rebound that stalls beneath the broken floor would provide further evidence that support is becoming resistance.

However, if the price breaks lower and quickly moves back into the range, sellers may have had their shot and missed. That would weaken the breakdown signal.

If buyers defend the support area again, the broader $80,106 to $87,374 range remains in play. The 100- and 200-bar moving averages on the four-hour chart would continue to provide intermediate decision points.

Let the levels guide the trade

The lesson is to separate the current bias from the next confirmation.

Repeated rejection at the 100-bar moving average favors sellers. A sustained break below the range floor would give them another victory. Until then, support buyers still have a chance to keep the battle inside the range.

In the video above, I explain how traders can use moving average resistance and swing support to define risk, judge control, and prepare for the next shove in Bitcoin.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canadian dollar touches an 18-month low as the US dollar jumps on hot CPI
item.description:
The US dollar is broadly stronger today and that briefly pushed it to the highest against the Canadian dollar since April 2025. The peak was 1.4299 (or 0.6993 CAD). The 70-cent level is a sensitive one domestically and a clean break of it could give Canadians another reason not to travel south this winter.

The loonie had made strong gains yesterday as the post-jobs report weakness reversed. Friday's data saw Canada unexpectedly shed jobs but a closer look showed it was driven by government job losses in healthcare and education. The latter is a category that's particularly hard to seasonally adjust for in September due to school restarting while neither is indicative of underlying economic strength. That said, there have been mixed indications on the Canadian economy and the housing sector in much of the country appears to be in the midst of another leg down.

Where it gets interesting is how central banks are reacting. In the year ahead, there are 97 basis points of hikes priced in for the Bank of Canada and 92 basis points for the Federal Reserve. Today's US CPI report narrowed that gap and if we see the Canadian economy stumble or the US accelerate further, then a real USD-positive divergence could open up.

Note that the starting points are already highly divergent with the Fed at 3.75-4.00% and the Bank of Canada at 2.25%. That extends further out the curve where Treasuries are paying notably more than Government of Canada bonds. 

As for the USD/CAD chart, it's telling that it's pushing through the 2026 highs. That doesn't leave much in the way of resistance until the Liberation Day peaks in the 1.45-1.47 range come into play. 

USDCAD weekly:

If we get into the mid-1.40s, I would be tempted to lean against that resistance as I expect the money to flow out of the US when the AI boom ebbs. A better trading relationship between Canada and the US could also turn the pair.

In terms of the fundamentals, the Canadian dollar has been buffered by commodity prices. Unfortunately, the Western Canadian Select oil discount has blown out recently, meaning that Canadian producers largely won't be getting global prices for their crude. PM Carney announced a new pipeline to the west coast but it will take 5-10 years to build after the usual Canadian court challenges and litigation.

For oil, the medium-term risks may be more to the downside if the US or Iran is forced to accept a peace in Hormuz. I tend to think the timelines for 'normalized' oil prices are long because of the extensive inventory rebuilding that will need to happen but any peace will be oil-negative for a time.

In terms of consumers, spending has held up well in both places and RBC today is out with fresh Canadian cardholder data for September. They note that core sales rose 0.5% m/m led by discretionary categories. Entertainment and arts spending increased 1.4%, travel rose 1%, and dining grew a more modest 0.3%.

High gasoline prices are obviously digging into budgets but so far they haven't cracked and that could give the Bank of Canada fodder to hike further from here. I'm skeptical that they will hike the four full hikes priced into the curve through 2027.

item.title: What technical levels are in play now for the broader US stock indices following the higher CPI data?

Until that break occurs, buyers still have a level to lean against and define their risk.

Nasdaq Composite: Between the hourly moving averages

The Nasdaq Composite has fallen below its 100-hour moving average at 27,168.43, giving sellers a short-term victory. However, the price remains above its rising 200-hour moving average at 26,820.47.

A failed break to a record high is a warning. A break below key support provides the next piece of evidence.

Sellers are making a play, but they still have work to do.

item.title: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
item.description:
The stakes around the October Federal Reserve meeting suddenly got much higher. 

Today's US CPI report was hot across the board, including in core measures that are less volatile than the energy-driven headline. The bond market quickly repriced on the data, with US 2-year yields now up 15 basis points on the day to 4.94%.

In the Fed funds futures market, pricing is now right at 50/50 for a hike or hold this month. It's also critical to note that the Fed goes into the blackout period on Saturday.

That leaves just three days to shape the narrative if the Fed doesn't want to go into the meeting with raised stakes. That starts today with a 1:30 pm ET speech from Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin. I'm a fan of Barkin's level-headed style and he usually represents the core views of the Fed, so that's one to watch especially closely. That said, we just heard from Barkin this week and he didn't offer much in the way of guidance.

One notable recent comment from him was in late September when he said that this cycle could be like the 1990s mid-cycle adjustment. Barkin was comparing now to an easing cycle in the 1990s, when Greenspan cut rates by 75 bps over seven months at the end of 1995. So by that analogue -- if you took it directly -- would be more dovish than what is priced in now. He also said he would not yet make an overheating case, but economy is firming and not weakening and that businesses feel they have pricing power.

I would not put it past him to tip towards the hawkish side but he's usually not the guy to make the first big wave.

Next on the calendar will be Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will appear on Yahoo Finance at 3 pm ET. He's candid but we have heard from him plenty and he has been leaning hawkish for awhile. That said, he hasn't been kicking down the door calling for rate hikes so if we see an incremental move in that direction today, it could be telling.

Tomorrow, we get to hear from the top guy with an 11:30 pm ET 'fireside chat' including Warsh at the IMF meetings. We will see if he sticks to his plan of not giving guidance or lets it out, my guess is that he will have to give a nod in one direction. Earlier that day, we will also hear from Hammack, who has been increasingly hawkish. 

The Friday calendar is currently bare of Fed speakers but we will monitor that for any changes.

In terms of economic data, we also get PPI and retail sales tomorrow so those will be key.

About half an hour before the US cash market opens, futures are trading near 7,828, having fallen sharply from the 7,870 area. Let's jump into my simple 4h chart S&P 500 futures chart:

Three observations stand out.

1. The earlier breakout was meaningful, but its momentum has faded.

After approximately five attempts, S&P 500 futures finally broke above the descending purple resistance line in early October. That breakout was subsequently tested around October 8-9, when price briefly pierced the former resistance before recovering.

This was constructive behavior. A previously troublesome resistance area appeared to be taking on a supporting role.

However, the subsequent rally stalled below the October 6 high near 7,897, leaving a lower high. The recovery was therefore losing some of its strength even before today's decline.

2. The rising channel has broken, potentially activating a bear flag.

The pitchfork drawn over the latest recovery also functions as a rising price channel. Following the sharp decline from the October 6 high, the subsequent advance took place within this upward-sloping structure.

That creates the possibility of a bear flag: a temporary recovery within a developing downward move.

Today's sharp drop below the channel's lower boundary is an early bearish development. It suggests that the recovery structure is failing, although the current four-hour candle is still developing.

A completed four-hour close beneath the channel, particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to reclaim its lower boundary, would strengthen the bearish interpretation.

3. Could the previous breakout line become the next downside destination?

The descending purple line, previously resistance and subsequently tested as support, now provides another area worth monitoring.

Its projected location is around 7,765-7,780near the current session, although the exact intersection changes with time.

This is not a confirmed downside target. It is a potential support test if the selloff continues.

For the immediate outlook, 7,870-7,880is an important recovery area. A sustained move back above it, accompanied by a reclaim of the broken channel boundary, would weaken the bear-flag interpretation.

The educational takeaway is that a breakout and a subsequent breakdown can both be meaningful without contradicting one another. The earlier breakout showed improving price structure, while today's channel failure suggests that improvement is now being challenged. The next retest and the subsequent follow-through matter more than either line crossing in isolation.

item.title: How to identify the economic data that really moves markets
item.description:
One of the biggest challenges for new traders is knowing which economic releases deserve the most attention. Economic calendars typically classify indicators as low, medium or high impact, but these labels can be misleading. A release marked as high impact can sometimes pass without moving markets much, while a low impact indicator can trigger a significant reaction.

The impact of economic data depends not only on the indicator itself, but also on the current economic environment, central bank focus and what the market has already priced in.

Why impact ratings on calendars are useless

Economic calendars generally assign impact ratings based on how much volatility an indicator has historically generated. However, historical volatility does not account for current context.

For example, US CPI is usually considered a high impact release because inflation plays a major role in the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions. But if inflation has been broadly stable and the Fed has made it clear that it is more concerned about the labour market, the same inflation report might generate a relatively muted reaction.

Conversely, a weaker than expected employment report could trigger a significant market move if traders are increasingly concerned about a deteriorating labour market and are looking for confirmation that the Fed will cut rates.

This is why traders should avoid relying exclusively on economic calendar labels. The question they should ask is: Which economic data could change expectations about future central bank decisions?

How to identify the economic data that matters

The best way to identify the most important economic releases is to understand what central banks are currently focusing on. Central banks make monetary policy decisions based on their assessment of inflation, economic growth, employment and financial conditions. However, the relative importance of these factors changes over time.

If inflation remains stubbornly high, policymakers may emphasize the need for convincing evidence that price pressures are easing before considering rate cuts. In that environment, inflation releases become particularly important because they can change expectations about how long interest rates will remain elevated.

For example, suppose Fed officials repeatedly highlight monthly core inflation as a key input in their decisions. In that case, US Core CPI M/M becomes the single most important release to watch. A reading significantly above consensus could increase expectations for tighter monetary policy, while a downside surprise could lead traders to price in fewer rate hikes or earlier rate cuts.

The market reaction will depend on how much the release changes the expected path of interest rates. A small deviation from consensus may have little impact, while a large surprise can force investors to reassess their outlook more aggressively.

The same principle applies when central banks are focused on employment. If policymakers begin expressing greater concern about a weakening labour market, indicators such as nonfarm payrolls and unemployment can become the main drivers of market volatility. The key is to follow the central bank's reaction function.

Economic indicators should never be looked at in isolation. Their importance depends on the economic context and the direction in which the economy is moving.

Imagine for example that inflation is too high, while PMIs suggest that economic activity remains strong. This combination can make central banks reluctant to ease monetary policy because demand remains resilient and inflationary pressures may persist.

In this situation, a stronger than expected PMI might not generate a particularly large reaction if the market already expects solid economic growth, unless the PMI surprises signficantly to the upside. A weaker than expected reading, however, could have a much greater impact.

Why? Because it would challenge the prevailing view that the economy is strong enough to sustain elevated interest rates. If growth starts slowing, demand and price pressures could eventually ease, giving the central bank more room to cut rates.

The opposite can also happen. If the economy is weakening and markets are increasingly concerned about recession, a stronger than expected PMI or employment report could trigger a significant reaction by reducing expectations for rate cuts.

The same economic release can therefore produce very different market reactions depending on the prevailing conditions.

Knowing what's already priced in is key

Even when you identify the right economic indicator, you still need to understand what the market expects before the release. Markets are forward-looking. Prices reflect investors' expectations about the future, and those expectations are constantly adjusted as new information arrives. As a result, markets generally react not to the data itself, but to how the data compares with what was expected and how it changes the future outlook.

Suppose inflation is expected to remain elevated, and traders have already priced in another interest rate hike. A report that confirms the consensus might not generate much volatility because it provides little new information.

Now imagine that inflation comes in significantly below expectations. This could challenge the assumption that further tightening is necessary, triggering a dovish repricing of interest rate expectations. Bond yields might fall, the currency could weaken and gold could rise, depending on the market context.

The reverse is also true. If markets have become excessively dovish and are pricing in several rate cuts, an inflation surprise to the upside could trigger a sharp hawkish repricing.

It is also important to consider positioning. If traders are already heavily positioned for a particular outcome, a release that supports that view can produce a limited reaction, or even a reversal, if the result fails to exceed expectations by enough.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

US CPI: Energy lifts the headline. What about the core?

The headline reading is expected to accelerate as higher energy prices work through the data. The more important question is how much of that pressure is spreading into other goods and services.

Last month, gasoline prices rose 3.9%, accounting for more than one-third of the monthly headline increase. Core inflation also rose 0.3%, with increases in airline fares, lodging and used vehicles.

A 0.2% monthly core reading would show some moderation from August, even if the annual rate rises to 2.5%. Those measures can move in different directions because the year-over-year reading also depends on the number dropping out from a year ago.

My focus will be on the core surprise:

  • Core at 0.3% or higher: That could push yields higher and support the dollar as traders reassess the risk of further Fed tightening.

  • Core in line at 0.2%: That could give the Fed more room to wait, particularly if the headline strength is concentrated in energy.

  • Core at 0.1% or lower: That would be moving in the right direction and could pressure yields and the dollar while providing some relief for stocks.

Thursday’s PPI report at 8:30 AM ET will add another piece to the inflation puzzle. Together, the reports will help economists refine their estimates for PCE and core PCE inflation.

item.title: Nasdaq analysis today as price is dancing around yesterday's close (but probably not for long)
item.description:
Nasdaq futures outlook today: Is the market building a bottom, or preparing for another leg lower?

October 14, 2026 | Nasdaq-100 E-mini futures (December 2026 contract, NQ) | US premarket analysis

Nasdaq futures are showing signs of stabilization following a sharp selloff, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to declare a durable market bottom.Buyers have defended the 30,705 area, while sellers have prevented a sustained recovery above approximately 30,890. For traders and investors, these two developments define an important test of whether the Nasdaq can recover or remains vulnerable to another decline.

The current technical outlook is moderately bearish, with meaningful evidence of buyers attempting to regain control.

Escalating Middle East friction and persistent supply risks continue to dictate sentiment across cross-asset markets. As Giuseppe Dellamotta at investingLive.com highlighted, crude oil extended its gains as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalated, driving WTI CFD contracts toward channel resistance near the $110 mark amid a reported strike on an administrative building at Saudi Aramco's Dhahran complex.

That persistent energy bid is spilling directly into broader risk appetite, with Giuseppe Dellamotta also noting that Ethereum remains under pressure from heavy spot ETF outflows and hawkish macro risks as traders defend the critical $2,360 support and trendline ahead of high-stakes U.S. CPI prints.

Yet even as geopolitical risk premia and higher yields loom over risk assets, growth narratives present a sharply divergent picture globally.

On Wall Street, as Eamonn Sheridan reported, UBS forecasts a blistering 28% Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth driven by AI and cyclicals, arguing that semiconductor demand and accelerating hyperscaler cloud revenue will insulate equities against rising freight and input costs.

Across the Pacific, however, the macro reality is far more subdued; as Justin Low at investingLive.com pointed out, China's September lending surprise masks a deeper slump in credit demand, where a 22% year-to-date contraction in bank loans underscores that households and businesses remain reluctant to leverage up despite Beijing's easing efforts. 

With that background music in mind, let's dive into today Nasdaq analysis at investingLive.com...

Nasdaq futures have recovered, but how much damage has been repaired?

The December 2026 Nasdaq-100 futures contract (NQ) declined from approximately 31,289 on October 12 to 30,591 on October 13.

That is a drop of roughly 698 points, or 2.2%, in a relatively short period.

The subsequent rebound reached approximately 30,889, recovering about 43% of that decline. This was a meaningful recovery, but it did not restore the market to its previous higher trading range.

The distinction matters.

A market can recover hundreds of points and still remain in a vulnerable technical position. The size of a rebound is only part of the story. Where the rebound stops, and what buyers can defend afterward, may tell us considerably more.

In this case, two important developments stand out:

  • Sellers reappeared around 30,889, preventing a stronger recovery.

  • Buyers subsequently defended the 30,705-30,725 region, without waiting for a return to the more significant historical support around 30,636.

These opposing forces help explain why a one-sided bullish or bearish assessment would be premature.

Why 30,889 is an important Nasdaq resistance level

The recovery toward 30,889 encountered an area associated with significant historical trading activity.

Rather than breaking decisively above that region and establishing a new, higher trading range, Nasdaq futures turned lower.

This suggests that sellers have not yet surrendered control of an important part of the recent decline.

For swing traders, the significance is not whether NQ can briefly trade above 30,889. It is whether buyers can establish a more durable recovery above approximately 30,890.

A sustained recovery above 30,890 would weaken the moderately bearish interpretation.

It would suggest that buyers are becoming more willing to accept higher prices and could open the door to a broader recovery.

By contrast, repeated failures below that level would reinforce the possibility that recent strength represents a temporary rebound within a larger corrective move.

An intermediate resistance region around 30,850-30,862 also deserves attention.

Together, these areas form a useful test of whether buyers are becoming more aggressive or whether rallies continue to encounter selling.

The bullish evidence: Buyers defended 30,705 before a deeper decline

One of the more constructive developments in the October 14 premarket session was the response around 30,705-30,725.

This area attracted buyers before price could revisit the important historical support around 30,636.

Following that defense, Nasdaq futures recovered toward 30,862, although sellers subsequently returned.

Why does this matter?

During a bearish trend, buyers often wait for increasingly lower prices before becoming willing to participate. When buying instead emerges at a higher level, it can be an early indication that demand is improving.

It does not establish a bottom on its own, but it warrants attention.

Consider the difference between three stages of a potential market recovery.

Stage 1: Buyers respond.A sharp decline attracts demand and prices bounce. This has already occurred.

Stage 2: Buyers establish a base.Subsequent declines begin stopping at higher levels, with sellers increasingly unable to drive the market to new lows. There are preliminary indications of this possibility, but it remains unconfirmed.

Stage 3: Buyers overcome resistance.The market begins sustaining trading above previous recovery highs. This is the more convincing evidence that the earlier bearish structure is changing.

The available analysis supports Stage 1, raises the possibility of Stage 2, and does not yet establish Stage 3.

For traders trying to identify a Nasdaq bottom, distinguishing these stages can be more useful than attempting to predict the exact lowest price.

Why 30,636 could become the next important test

The area around 30,636 is another significant historical support reference.

It originally attracted attention because of an older concentration of trading activity dating from October 1. The October 12-13 decline subsequently revisited this area, with the market trading around and below it before recovering.

That makes it a meaningful reference for evaluating the next potential downside move.

If NQ breaks below the recently defended 30,705 region, a return toward 30,636 becomes a more credible scenario.

What happens there would be important.

A successful defense could strengthen the interpretation that Nasdaq futures are establishing a broader trading range or bottoming structure.

A sustained breakdown, particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to recover 30,636, would instead suggest that sellers retain the advantage.

An important educational point:Support is not a guaranteed price floor. Its value is that it gives traders a location where the market's response can help confirm or challenge their expectations.

What happens if Nasdaq futures break below 30,636?

Below that area, the next significant region in the supplied analysis is approximately 30,540-30,567.

Several historical trading references converge there, making it a potentially important area of interest during a renewed decline.

Another historical reference sits around 30,500, associated with earlier trading activity that helped establish a higher market range.

These should be viewed as areas where a market reaction may occur, rather than guaranteed targets or automatic buying opportunities.

The distinction becomes especially relevant in a market that has recently experienced sharp selling.

A trader anticipating a bounce around 30,550, for example, still faces the possibility of a sustained breakdown. The existence of historical support does not remove that risk.

For investors, a decline into this deeper region would signal additional deterioration in the Nasdaq's short-term structure, even if the longer-term investment outlook for individual technology companies remained unchanged.

Three scenarios for Nasdaq traders

Scenario 1: Bearish continuation

NQ loses the 30,705-30,725 buyer-defense zone and fails to recover it. This would increase the relevance of a test of 30,636.

If 30,636 also gives way on a sustained basis, the next regions to monitor become 30,540-30,567 and approximately 30,500.

What weakens this scenario: Buyers reclaim the broken support areas and eventually establish a sustained recovery above 30,890.

Scenario 2: A developing market bottom

Buyers defend the 30,705 region, future pullbacks establish higher lows, and NQ begins recovering the 30,850-30,890 resistance area.

This would suggest that the market is repairing the damage from the preceding decline.

What weakens this scenario: Another sustained breakdown below 30,705, particularly if 30,636 subsequently fails.

Scenario 3: Continued sideways consolidation

Buyers repeatedly defend lower prices while sellers reject attempts to recover the previous trading range.

This could produce a series of reversals that frustrate traders attempting to follow a directional move.

Practical implication: Waiting for a clearer break or a successful retest may offer better information than anticipating every move within the range.

Key Nasdaq futures levels to watch

December 2026 NQ contract | October 14 premarket snapshot | Approximate levels

The hierarchy matters more than treating every point as equally significant.

For traders watching the next several sessions, the most important questions concern the durability of 30,705, the response to a potential test of 30,636, and whether buyers can eventually overcome the resistance around 30,890.

These are NQ futures price references, not interchangeable order levels for the Nasdaq Composite, QQQ ETF or individual technology stocks.

What today's broader market environment adds

The technical uncertainty comes during a period in which technology shares are sensitive to developments in artificial intelligence, semiconductor competition and interest-rate expectations.

Wednesday's premarket reporting indicated that Nasdaq futures were relatively steady while investors assessed developments in chipmakers, bank earnings and upcoming US inflation figures.

The earnings outlook for semiconductor companies, including ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor, was also attracting attention.

This matters because an improving Nasdaq technical structure could be reinforced by stronger participation among its influential technology constituents.

Conversely, renewed pressure on major semiconductor and growth stocks could make a sustained recovery more difficult, particularly if accompanied by higher bond yields or renewed concern about inflation.

These are potential influences, not evidence that any particular news event caused the specific price reactions identified in this analysis.

Three practical lessons for swing traders

1. A market bottom is a process, not necessarily a price.

The first rebound after a selloff may be impressive, but evidence of a durable bottom generally becomes stronger when buyers defend higher lows and overcome important resistance.

2. Use technical levels to test an opinion, not defend it indefinitely.

A moderately bearish outlook makes sense while resistance holds and the recovery remains incomplete. But if NQ establishes sustained trading above 30,890, that assessment should be reconsidered.

Similarly, the defense of 30,705 is constructive only for as long as subsequent price behavior supports that interpretation.

3. Trade management can matter more than predicting the next move.

Traders operating with multiple profit objectives may consider reducing exposure when significant targets or support and resistance areas are reached.

After meaningful partial profits, reducing remaining risk or moving a protective stop toward entry can sometimes be appropriate.

However, Nasdaq futures can experience substantial short-term volatility. Moving a stop too aggressively can cause an otherwise valid trade to close prematurely.

Position sizing, stop placement and the intended holding period should be considered together.

What should Nasdaq stock investors take away?

For investors holding technology stocks, semiconductor companies or broader Nasdaq-linked funds, the futures market provides a useful indication of near-term market risk appetite.

However, the importance of a Nasdaq futures support level depends on the investor's horizon.

A day trader might regard a sustained break of 30,705 as an important change requiring an immediate reassessment.

An investor with a six-month or multi-year horizon may instead use the same development to assess broader market conditions while focusing primarily on company earnings, valuations, competitive positioning and longer-term growth prospects.

A weakening index does not imply that every component company has become a poor investment. Equally, a strong index rebound does not establish that every underlying stock is attractively valued.

Bottom line: The Nasdaq has shown resilience, but has not confirmed a bottom

The Nasdaq's recent recovery is significant enough to challenge an overly pessimistic outlook, particularly because buyers defended the 30,705 region without allowing another immediate test of the earlier lows.

Nevertheless, the failure around 30,889 remains an important warning that the bearish structure has not yet been convincingly repaired.

For now, the evidence favors continued caution rather than a definitive bullish reversal call.

Above 30,890, the recovery argument becomes more convincing. Below 30,705, the risk of a renewed decline toward 30,636 increases.

Between those areas, the market may continue testing the patience of both bulls and bears.

The Nasdaq is providing clues about where it may go next, but traders and investors should remain prepared to change their interpretation as those clues evolve.

Educational market analysis, not personalized investment advice. Trading futures involves substantial risk of loss.

item.title: China's September lending surprise masks a much deeper slump in credit demand
item.description:
China's new bank loans climbed to ¥1.08 trillion in September, beating market expectations of ¥975 billion. At first glance, that seems like a welcome improvement especially after the rather dismal lending figures we've seen over the past few months. That being said, lending is still down roughly 16% compared to September last year. And adding to that, the year-on-date snapshot isn't pretty either.

In looking at the first nine months of 2026, Chinese banks have now extended ¥11.52 trillion in new loans during this period. That falls short when viewed in comparison to the ¥14.75 trillion over the same period last year. In short, we're looking at a rather substantial 22% decline in new lending this year.

I would argue that the figures above tell us quite a bit about the state of China's domestic economy.

The problem that China is facing right now is not that banks aren't willing to lend. It is more of a case that households and businesses aren't particularly eager to borrow in the first place.

A big part of that can be traced back to the property market crash that unfolded in 2021. With the property sector still struggling to this day, households have little incentive to take on new mortgages. Meanwhile, businesses aren't exactly rushing to expand operations when domestic consumption remains sluggish.

Even the PBOC itself has already acknowledged that slower loan growth could become the new normal, as declining borrowing from the property sector and local government financing vehicles outweighs demand from emerging industries.

As such, I wouldn't read too much into the improvement from the September figure today. It needs to be put into context as China's credit recovery remains very much an uphill battle.

Sure, Beijing can make borrowing cheaper and encourage banks to lend. However, to convince households and businesses to actually take on more debt is a whole other matter.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
